prompt: By the lesson, when is a technical decision a product decision?
hint: Look at who feels the outcome, not who types it.

choices.text: When product asked for the feature it belongs to
choices.why: The seat hold belongs to no feature request and is still product's; origin is not the test.

choices.text: When it costs more than a sprint of work
choices.why: The seat hold is one setting; size of the work says nothing about who feels the result.

choices.text: When users feel it or the business carries it
choices.why: Right: whoever types it in, a choice felt by buyers or venues is a product decision.

choices.text: When it touches the user interface
choices.why: A database setting changed what buyers saw without touching a screen.

prompt: Coreto shortens the seat hold everywhere. Who is hurt first?
hint: Somebody still in the middle of paying.

choices.text: Venues, whose shows look sold out while seats are unpaid
choices.why: That is the longer hold's failure: seats sit with buyers who walked away.

choices.text: The database team
choices.why: A shorter hold helps the database: fewer locks pile up during the rush.

choices.text: Nobody, since the change is technical
choices.why: That is the disguise: a setting in a configuration file that decides which buyers lose.

choices.text: A buyer still typing a card number
choices.why: Right: a shorter hold expires on the slow buyer, and on a popular show the seat is gone for good.

prompt: Match each decision, as it was raised, to what it actually decides.
hint: Follow each one to the person who feels it.

pairs.left: How long Catalogue caches seat availability
pairs.right: Whether buyers are shown seats already gone

pairs.left: How long buyer data is kept
pairs.right: Legal exposure, and whether last year's tickets are visible
What Coreto promises venues, and what it costs engineering

pairs.left: Whether Box Office scans with no network
pairs.right: A queue at the door, or a ticket admitted twice

right_distractors: Which index the reservations table gets

prompt: A longer seat hold makes the seat map show a show as sold out. Why is that a problem for the venue, not only for buyers?
hint: What happens when the holds expire?

choices.text: A false sell-out, then unplanned late sales
choices.why: Right: fans give up, and seats return to whoever happens to be refreshing when the holds expire.

choices.text: The venue is charged for every held seat
choices.why: The lesson describes no such charge; the harm is in how the sale unfolds.

choices.text: The longer hold makes the database fail at 10:00
choices.why: Locks do pile up, but the question is what the venue sees; a false sell-out is its harm.

choices.text: Venues prefer short holds as a rule
choices.why: The lesson gives venues no fixed preference; that is why their view is asked for in the note.

prompt: Box Office's scanner loses the network at a venue's door. Which pair of consequences is the real choice?
hint: A copy on the device cannot see the other doors.

choices.text: Slower scans, or a bigger phone battery
choices.why: Those are engineering details; the choice the venue feels is about its queue and its tickets.

choices.text: A queue outside, or a copied ticket let in twice
choices.why: Right: stop entry until the network returns, or scan against a local copy that cannot see another door.

choices.text: Losing the sale, or refunding the buyer
choices.why: The ticket is already sold; the choice happens at the door, not at checkout.

choices.text: Higher cloud cost, or a new on-call shift for Box Office
choices.why: Neither is what the venue experiences on the night; the lesson's pair is.

prompt: Which of these are marks of a disguised product decision? Choose all that apply.
hint: Five marks in the lesson; three are here.

choices.text: A default is about to be accepted
choices.why: Right: nobody chose it, and it is still a choice.

choices.text: The change needs a database migration
choices.why: A migration is engineering work; it says nothing about who feels the outcome.

choices.text: Somebody says "it depends what we want"
choices.why: Right: the decision turns on a goal, and its owners are not in the room.

choices.text: Both options are technically sound
choices.why: Right: the remaining disagreement is about who bears a cost.

choices.text: The code is in the reservation module
choices.why: Most changes in that module are engineering's; the place is not the mark.

prompt: Which of these decisions belongs to engineering alone?
hint: Nobody outside would ever notice the answer.

choices.text: How long a seat is held
choices.why: Buyers feel it at the payment step; it carries a mark.

choices.text: How long buyer data is kept
choices.why: Buyers and a regulator see the result; it is product's and legal's too.

choices.text: How stale the seat map may be
choices.why: A stale map shows buyers seats that are gone; it carries a mark.

choices.text: Which index the holds table gets
choices.why: Right: it carries none of the five marks, and asking product would waste everybody's time.

prompt: Catalogue's availability cache lifetime came from a library ___ that nobody had set on purpose.
hint: What a setting is before anybody changes it.

prompt: A team, having learnt this lesson, now sends every choice to product, down to the test framework. What does the lesson say is wrong with that?

choices.text: Product will decide badly on technical questions
choices.why: Quality of the answer is not the lesson's objection; the waste and the lesson taught to product are.

choices.text: Nothing; more consultation is always safer
choices.why: The lesson names this the opposite mistake: it buries the disguised decisions among trivial ones.

choices.text: It wastes time and undermines engineering's autonomy
choices.why: Right: a choice with none of the marks is engineering's, and saying so protects its autonomy.

choices.text: Test frameworks need approval from the CTO, not product
choices.why: No approval is needed at all: it carries no mark, so the team decides.

prompt: Davi's list says who should decide each disguised decision with engineering. Why does engineering stay in the room?

choices.text: It has the final vote on anything in the code
choices.why: The lesson gives product the choice; engineering's part is different.

choices.text: To make sure the default is kept
choices.why: An accepted default is one of the marks; keeping it is not engineering's job here.

choices.text: Only it knows each option's cost under load
choices.why: Right: product owns the outcome, and the options only exist as engineering describes them.

choices.text: Because the decision will be written as code
choices.why: Who implements it was never the test; what engineering knows about the options is the reason.

prompt: "We need to shorten the hold or the database will fall over during on-sales." What is wrong with framing it this way?
hint: What does Júlia not get to see?

choices.text: It is too technical for product
choices.why: The sentence is short and plain; its fault is what it leaves out.

choices.text: It hides the trade, so product approves something it did not see
choices.why: Right: Júlia agrees to a database fix and learns from a venue that buyers are losing seats.

choices.text: It exaggerates the risk to the database
choices.why: The risk is real; the problem is presenting one option as the only one.

choices.text: It should be addressed to the CTO
choices.why: The consequences fall on buyers and venues, which are Júlia's.

prompt: Put the parts of Davi and Mateus's note to Júlia in the order they appear.
hint: The options come before the view on them.
items: Why the decision is needed now
The options, each with its consequences
The date an answer is needed by
trap: Putting the recommendation first turns the options into a defence of it, which is the necessity framing at greater length.

prompt: Why must a note about data retention say in its first paragraph which options can be undone, when the seat-hold note could leave it near the end?
hint: Can a later decision bring deleted records back?

choices.text: Retention is a legal matter, and legal notes have a fixed format
choices.why: The lesson's reason is about reversibility, not about document formats.

choices.text: Deleted records cannot be restored
choices.why: Right: a shorter retention period is irreversible once it runs, so it deserves more care up front; the hold options are one setting apart.

choices.text: Product reads only the first paragraph
choices.why: The lesson assumes Júlia reads the note; the point is how much care each decision deserves.

choices.text: Retention has more options than the seat hold
choices.why: The number of options is not the difference; whether they can be undone is.

prompt: Júlia picks the option the note warned against. By the lesson, what does engineering do?
hint: Who owns the choice, and who owns the consequences' honesty?

choices.text: Escalates to the CTO until the decision is reversed
choices.why: Product owns the choice; escalating a fairly framed decision undoes the point of framing it.

choices.text: Builds the recommended option anyway
choices.why: That would take the decision back by stealth, which is worse than never framing it.

choices.text: Asks product to sign a waiver
choices.why: The note itself is the record; nothing more formal is asked for.

choices.text: Builds it; the warning is on record
choices.why: Right: product owns the choice and engineering owns the honesty of the consequences, which the note already supplied.

prompt: Coreto's partner API has no limit on requests per partner, and Payments proposes one. Which question decides whether this is a disguised product decision?
hint: Run the marks: who feels a limit when it bites?

choices.text: Which rate-limiting library Payments would use
choices.why: That is the implementation beneath the decision, and it is engineering's.

choices.text: Whether the limit can be set in configuration
choices.why: The seat hold is in configuration too; where a value lives does not decide who feels it.

choices.text: How long the change would take to build
choices.why: Size of work is not a mark; a one-line change was the lesson's main example.

choices.text: Whether someone outside the company would be turned away
choices.why: Right: a number a customer feels and a failure a customer sees are two of the marks.

prompt: An engineer proposes that a password-reset link should expire sooner, for security. Framed for product, which consequence belongs in the note?
hint: Describe it by who feels it.

choices.text: The token lifetime drops in the authentication service
choices.why: That is the technical change, not a consequence anybody outside engineering can weigh.

choices.text: The change is a single line
choices.why: Effort belongs in the note, but it is not the consequence product is choosing between.

choices.text: A buyer who opens the e-mail late has to ask for a new link
choices.why: Right: written in the words of the person who feels it, beside the security gain on the other side.

choices.text: Security has approved it already
choices.why: An approval is not a consequence; it is the necessity framing in another voice.

prompt: By the lesson, product owns the choice; engineering owns the ___ of the consequences.
A note to product ends with "so what do you want us to do?" after a page on lock timeouts and connection pools. How does the lesson classify it?
hint: One of the two habits that get in the way.

choices.text: A good note, since it hands product the decision
choices.why: It hands over a question product cannot weigh, so the decision stays with engineering by default.

choices.text: The necessity framing
choices.why: The necessity framing conceals the options; this one buries them.

choices.text: A technical briefing that buries the choice
choices.why: Right: with no options in the reader's words, product cannot decide and the default wins.

choices.text: A decision record
choices.why: A record writes down a decision taken; this note never reaches one.

prompt: Where does the lesson send you for how error budgets turn an availability target into an agreement between product and engineering?

choices.text: Lesson 17 of this course
choices.why: Lesson 17 is about decision records, where a disguised decision gets written down.

choices.text: `delivery-metrics` lesson 16
choices.why: Right: this lesson only shows the target is not engineering's to pick alone.

choices.text: `people-leadership` lesson 22
choices.why: That lesson covers conflict with product, which follows a disagreement over a note.

choices.text: `architect-communication` lesson 4
choices.why: That lesson is about turning technical risk into business risk in general.
